history.heading: A court archive in brass
paragraphs: The objects called Benin Bronzes were made mostly of brass, and also of ivory, wood and coral, by guilds that worked for the Oba, the king of Benin. The casters' guild, the Igun Eronmwon, still works in Igun Street in Benin City today, and its members trace their craft back to the thirteenth or fourteenth century.

The rectangular plaques, cast from the sixteenth century onwards, were nailed to the wooden pillars of the royal palace. They show Obas, chiefs, warriors, musicians and Portuguese traders, and together they worked as a record of the court's history. Commemorative heads stood on royal altars dedicated to past Obas.

In February 1897 a British force attacked Benin City in reprisal for the killing of a British party that had tried to reach the city against the Oba's wishes. The palace was burned, Oba Ovonramwen was exiled, and several thousand objects were taken. Many were sold to cover the costs of the expedition, which is why they are now spread over more than 150 museums.

geography.heading: From the palace to 150 museums
paragraphs: Benin City lies in the rainforest belt of southern Nigeria, in today's Edo State, about 300 kilometres east of Lagos. It has nothing to do with the modern Republic of Benin, which took its name from the Bight of Benin, the bay of the Atlantic along this coast.

At its height the kingdom was surrounded by earthworks thousands of kilometres long, and its capital was laid out in wards for the different guilds. Its trade reached the coast through rivers and creeks, where it met Portuguese, Dutch and British merchants.

After 1897 the objects travelled by river and sea to London, and from there to auction houses and museums in Britain, Germany, Austria, the United States and elsewhere. Some have now come back: Germany transferred ownership of its Benin collections to Nigeria in 2022.

current.institution: British Museum (and more than 150 other collections)

removal.event: Seized in the British attack on Benin City, 1897

history.heading: A stone that passed between empires
paragraphs: The Koh-i-Noor, whose name means 'Mountain of Light' in Persian, was probably mined in the Deccan in southern India, where the Kollur mines supplied many famous diamonds. Its early history is a mix of legend and later accounts; the first reliable descriptions come from the Mughal court in the seventeenth century, when it was set in Shah Jahan's Peacock Throne.

In 1739 the Persian ruler Nader Shah sacked Delhi and took the Peacock Throne and the diamond to Iran. After his murder it passed to the Afghan Durrani dynasty, and in 1813 Maharaja Ranjit Singh, founder of the Sikh Empire, obtained it from the exiled Afghan ruler Shah Shuja.

After the British defeated the Sikhs, the Treaty of Lahore of 1849 required the ten-year-old Maharaja Duleep Singh to surrender the stone to Queen Victoria. It was cut down from about 186 to 105.6 carats in 1852 and is now set in a crown of the British Crown Jewels. India, Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran have each been named as claimants.

geography.heading: Golconda, Delhi, Kabul, Lahore, London
paragraphs: The diamond's route crosses South and Central Asia: from the Deccan to the Mughal capitals of Agra and Delhi, west to Iran, north to Kabul and Kandahar, and back east to Lahore, the capital of the Sikh Empire in the Punjab.

Lahore, where the diamond was handed over in 1849, is now the second city of Pakistan; the partition of 1947 divided the Punjab between India and Pakistan. That is one reason why its 'country of origin' is disputed.
From Lahore the stone travelled to Bombay and by ship to Britain, where it was shown at the Great Exhibition of 1851 in London. Today it is kept in the Jewel House at the Tower of London.

removal.event: Surrendered under the Treaty of Lahore after the Anglo-Sikh war, 1849

history.heading: The garden of perfect brightness
paragraphs: The Yuanmingyuan, the 'Garden of Perfect Brightness', was the main residence of the Qing emperors from the early eighteenth century. It was a vast complex of lakes, pavilions, libraries and palaces, including European-style buildings designed by Jesuit missionaries, and it held one of the richest collections of art and books in China.

In October 1860, at the end of the Second Opium War, British and French troops looted the palace. Days later the British envoy Lord Elgin, son of the man who removed the Parthenon sculptures, ordered it burned in reprisal for the torture and killing of prisoners. The fires lasted for days.

Porcelain, bronzes, jades, textiles and books were divided among soldiers, sold at auction on the spot and later in London and Paris. Empress Eugénie displayed a large share at Fontainebleau. The ruins, left in place, are now a memorial park in Beijing.

geography.heading: North-west of Beijing, far from home
paragraphs: The garden lay about eight kilometres north-west of the walled city of Beijing, in a landscape of springs and hills that the Qing emperors turned into imperial parks, together with the nearby Summer Palace (Yiheyuan), which was rebuilt after later destruction.

Looted objects left through the port of Tianjin and by ship to Europe. They are now in the British Museum and the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, at Fontainebleau near Paris, and in many private collections; Chinese estimates speak of more than a million objects lost in total.
Today the Yuanmingyuan ruins, with the broken stone arches of the European palaces, are one of the most visited memorials in China, and the site of annual commemorations.

current.institution: British Museum, Victoria and Albert Museum, Château de Fontainebleau and others

removal.event: Looted by British and French troops, 1860

history.heading: A Buddha from the Pala world
paragraphs: The Sultanganj Buddha is a standing figure of the Buddha about 2.3 metres tall, cast in copper in sections around a clay core. It is dated to roughly 500–700 CE, between the late Gupta period and the rise of the Pala kings, when eastern India was a great centre of Buddhist learning.

The figure raises its right hand in the gesture of reassurance, and its robe clings to the body in fine, rippling folds typical of the sculpture of this period. It is one of the largest surviving metal statues from ancient India.

It was found in 1861–1862 by E. B. Harris, a British engineer building the East Indian Railway, in the ruins of a monastery at Sultanganj. He shipped it to Britain, and in 1864 it was bought for Birmingham, where it is in the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery.

geography.heading: On the Ganges, in Bihar
paragraphs: Sultanganj is a town on the south bank of the Ganges in Bihar, in eastern India, not far from the ruins of the great Buddhist university of Vikramashila. Bihar, whose name comes from 'vihara', a Buddhist monastery, is where the Buddha lived and taught.

The river was the main highway of the region, linking monasteries and trading towns, and it later guided the route of the East Indian Railway, whose construction brought British engineers into the area.
From Bihar the statue went down the Ganges to Calcutta and by sea to Britain. It is now about 7,500 kilometres away from the place where it was found.

removal.event: Removed by a British railway engineer, 1861–1862

history.heading: Sculpture for Athena
paragraphs: The Parthenon was built on the Acropolis of Athens between 447 and 432 BCE as a temple to Athena, under the direction of Pericles, with sculpture designed by Phidias. Its decoration had three parts: the frieze around the inner building, showing a procession; the metopes, panels showing battles of gods, heroes, Lapiths and centaurs; and the pediments, with the birth of Athena and her contest with Poseidon.
Over two thousand years the building was a church, a mosque and, in 1687, an Ottoman gunpowder store that exploded when Venetian forces shelled it. Much of the sculpture was damaged or scattered.

Between 1801 and 1812 agents of Lord Elgin, British ambassador to the Ottoman court, removed about half of the surviving sculpture, citing a permit whose original text has never been found. The British government bought the collection in 1816. Greece, independent from 1830, has asked for its return since the nineteenth century.

geography.heading: From the Acropolis to Bloomsbury
paragraphs: The Acropolis is a limestone hill rising about 70 metres above central Athens, the city's sacred centre since the Bronze Age. From the Parthenon the view reaches the sea at Piraeus and the island of Salamis.

Elgin's crates travelled from Athens to Piraeus and by sea to Britain; one ship, the Mentor, sank off the island of Kythira in 1802, and its cargo was recovered by divers. In London the sculptures went on display in the British Museum in Bloomsbury, where they are shown in the Duveen Gallery.

In Athens, the Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009 at the foot of the hill, displays the sculptures that stayed in Greece, with plaster casts marking those in London, and a glass gallery facing the Parthenon itself.

removal.event: Removed by Lord Elgin's agents under a disputed Ottoman permit, 1801–1812

history.heading: Astronomy for the emperor
paragraphs: In imperial China, predicting eclipses and fixing the calendar were duties of the state, carried out by the Bureau of Astronomy. The observatory on the city wall of Beijing was founded in 1442 and remained in use for almost five centuries.

In 1673 the Flemish Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest, head of the Bureau under the Kangxi Emperor, had six new bronze instruments cast: armillary spheres, a celestial globe, a quadrant, a sextant and an altazimuth. More were added in the eighteenth century, the last in 1744.

After the Boxer War of 1900, French and German troops took instruments as trophies. France returned its share in 1902. The German share, shown at Potsdam, came back in 1921 under Article 131 of the Treaty of Versailles, the same treaty that gave German rights in Shandong to Japan, which led China to refuse to sign it.

geography.heading: A tower on the old city wall
paragraphs: The observatory stands on a bastion at the south-eastern corner of the Ming inner city wall, near today's Jianguomen. From its platform the astronomers had an open view of the sky above the flat city.
In 1900 the instruments were split between the French legation in Beijing and Potsdam, near Berlin, more than 7,000 kilometres away, where they stood in the gardens of the royal palaces.
Most of Beijing's walls were demolished in the twentieth century for the Second Ring Road and the underground; the observatory tower survived and is now a museum with the instruments back on top.

removal.event: Seized by French and German troops, 1900

history.heading: An ancestor and a birdman
paragraphs: Hoa Hakananai'a is a moai, one of the monumental figures that the Rapa Nui people carved to embody their ancestors. Unlike most moai, which are made of soft volcanic tuff, it is carved from hard basalt and is about 2.4 metres tall. Its name is usually translated as 'stolen' or 'hidden friend'.

It stood inside a stone house at Orongo, the ceremonial village of the Tangata Manu, or Birdman, cult. On its back are later carvings of birdmen, frigate birds and ceremonial paddles, which record how the Rapa Nui changed their religion after the age of moai building.

In 1868 the crew of the British ship HMS Topaze took it, with the help of islanders whose consent is unknown, and it was presented to Queen Victoria, who gave it to the British Museum. In 2018 a delegation from Rapa Nui asked for its return; the museum has proposed loans.

geography.heading: The navel of the world
paragraphs: Rapa Nui is one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth, about 3,700 kilometres from the coast of Chile and 2,000 kilometres from Pitcairn, its nearest inhabited neighbour. Its people, of Polynesian origin, call it Te Pito o te Henua, 'the navel of the world'.

Orongo sits on the rim of the Rano Kau volcano, above cliffs that drop to the sea, facing the islet of Motu Nui, where each year competitors swam to collect the first sooty tern egg of the season in the Birdman contest.

Chile annexed the island in 1888. Rapa Nui National Park has been a World Heritage Site since 1995, and since 2017 it has been managed by the Rapa Nui community. Hoa Hakananai'a is now in London, some 14,000 kilometres away.

removal.event: Taken by the crew of HMS Topaze, 1868

history.heading: A throne of power
paragraphs: King Glele ruled Dahomey from 1858 to 1889. The kingdom, with its capital at Abomey, was known for its centralised state, its army that included a corps of women soldiers, and its role in the Atlantic slave trade, which it continued into the nineteenth century.

Thrones like Glele's, carved in wood and decorated with metal, were royal regalia shown in ceremonies; sculptures and reliefs in the palaces told the history of each reign through symbols chosen by the kings. Glele's emblem was the lion.

In 1892 French troops under General Alfred Dodds conquered Dahomey. The royal palaces were burned, and throne, statues and doors were taken to Paris. In 2021, after a law passed by the French parliament, France returned 26 of these royal treasures to the Republic of Benin.

geography.heading: Abomey and the coast
paragraphs: Abomey lies inland in the south of today's Republic of Benin, about 100 kilometres from the Atlantic coast, where the ports of Ouidah and Porto-Novo linked the kingdom to European traders.

The Royal Palaces of Abomey, a group of earthen palaces built by successive kings, have been a World Heritage Site since 1985. The Republic of Benin took its name in 1975 from the Bight of Benin, the bay along its coast.

Taken to Paris in the 1890s, the treasures were shown at the Trocadéro and from 2006 at the Musée du quai Branly. Since their return they have been exhibited in Cotonou, and a new museum is planned in Abomey.

removal.event: Seized by French troops in the conquest of Dahomey, 1892

alt.long_description: An Inca ceramic aryballos in burnished red-brown clay, with a narrow neck, flared rim, two side handles and a vertical band of cream and dark diamond and zigzag motifs, on a grey background.

history.heading: Objects of an Inca estate
paragraphs: The Yale collections from Machu Picchu include painted ceramics in the imperial Inca style, bronze and silver pins and tools, stone objects and the remains of more than a hundred people from burial caves around the site. Studies of the bones showed that many people there came from distant parts of the empire, brought to serve the royal household.
The estate was built around 1450 for the ruler Pachacuti and used for a few generations. After the Spanish conquest it lost its purpose, but people in the valley kept farming and living there.

The export of the objects was authorised by Peru in 1912 and 1916 as a loan for study. After a lawsuit filed in 2008 and an agreement in 2010, Yale returned them in 2011–2012 to Cusco, where they are shown in the Casa Concha.

geography.heading: Between the Andes and the Amazon
paragraphs: Machu Picchu stands on a ridge at about 2,400 metres above sea level, above a bend of the Urubamba River, where the Andes descend towards the Amazon basin. The climate is warmer and wetter than in Cusco, and the slopes are covered in cloud forest.

Roads linked the estate to Cusco and to other royal sites in the Urubamba valley, the 'Sacred Valley' of the Incas. Today a railway follows the river from Cusco and Ollantaytambo to the town of Aguas Calientes at the foot of the site.
The objects went to New Haven, Connecticut, some 6,000 kilometres away, and came back in 2011–2012. The historic sanctuary has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

removal.event: Excavated by Yale expeditions and exported as a loan, 1912–1916

history.heading: One of West Africa's oldest sculptural traditions
paragraphs: The Nok culture flourished in central Nigeria in the first millennium BCE and the early centuries CE. Its people were farmers and among the earliest iron smelters in West Africa, and they made life-size and smaller terracotta figures with elaborate hairstyles, jewellery and triangular or D-shaped eyes.

The first Nok terracotta was found by tin miners at the village of Nok in 1943, and the archaeologist Bernard Fagg collected many more. Scholars still debate what the figures meant: ancestors, rulers, or figures for rituals.

Because the figures fetched high prices, looters dug up hundreds of sites from the 1990s, destroying the context that would explain them. Nigeria bans their export; some have been seized and returned, but many are in private collections and museums abroad.

geography.heading: The Jos Plateau and the valleys below
paragraphs: Nok sites are spread over a large area of central Nigeria, in today's Kaduna, Plateau and Nasarawa states, on the southern and western edges of the Jos Plateau, a highland of granite hills rich in tin.
The terracottas were made from local clay and fired in open fires. Many have been found in river gravels and in pits, sometimes broken and deliberately buried.
Looted figures left Nigeria through regional trading networks and reached dealers in Europe and North America. Today the National Museum in Jos and the museum in Lagos hold important collections.

current.institution: Museums and private collections in Europe and North America

removal.event: Dug up illegally and sold abroad, above all from the 1990s

alt.long_description: A fragment of a relief from Persepolis: a bearded Achaemenid official in a rounded cap and long robe walks in profile beneath a frieze of twelve-petalled rosettes.

images/achaemenid.jpg.alt: Grey limestone relief of a Persian courtier in profile, with a curled beard and cap, below a band of rosettes.
images/achaemenid.jpg.long_description: A fragment of a relief from Persepolis: a bearded Achaemenid official in a rounded cap and long robe walks in profile beneath a frieze of twelve-petalled rosettes.

images/achaemenid2.jpg.alt: Limestone relief fragment from Persepolis showing two Persian figures in long robes, one carrying an object.
images/achaemenid2.jpg.long_description: A broken slab of pale limestone carved with two figures in profile wearing long pleated robes, from a procession on the stairways of Persepolis.

images/achaemenid3.jpg.alt: Relief of a winged sphinx with a human head and crown, framed by a lotus plant and rosettes.
images/achaemenid3.jpg.long_description: An Achaemenid stone relief of a seated winged creature with the body of a lion and a bearded human head wearing a crown, facing a stylised plant, with a border of rosettes below.

history.heading: The ceremonial capital of an empire
paragraphs: Persepolis, which the Persians called Parsa, was founded by Darius I around 518 BCE as a ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire. Its terraces and halls were decorated with reliefs of guards, courtiers and delegations from the empire's peoples, from Ethiopians to Indians and Ionians, bringing gifts to the king.
The reliefs were carved in local grey limestone and originally painted. They present the empire as an ordered world in harmony under the king, rather than scenes of conquest.

Alexander the Great burned Persepolis in 330 BCE. From the seventeenth century European travellers described the ruins, and in the nineteenth century diplomats and travellers removed fragments, some now in the British Museum. Others were taken in the twentieth century and sold; a relief seized in New York in 2017 was returned to Iran.

geography.heading: The plain of Marvdasht
paragraphs: Persepolis lies on the plain of Marvdasht in Fars province, south-western Iran, about 60 kilometres north-east of Shiraz, at the foot of the Kuh-e Rahmat, the 'Mountain of Mercy'.
Fars, the ancient Persis, was the homeland of the Achaemenid dynasty. Nearby are Pasargadae, the earlier capital of Cyrus the Great, and Naqsh-e Rostam, with the rock-cut tombs of the kings.
Persepolis has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. Fragments of its reliefs are scattered across museums in London, Paris, Berlin, New York, Chicago and elsewhere.

removal.event: Taken by European diplomats and travellers in the 19th century; others later looted and sold

alt.long_description: Side view of the bust of Nefertiti: smooth skin painted in warm tones, a finely outlined eye, red lips and a tall flat-topped blue crown with a gold band, against a pale blue background.

images/cropped-nefertiti1.jpg.alt: Close-up profile of the painted bust of Nefertiti: long neck, dark outlined eye, red lips and blue crown.
images/cropped-nefertiti1.jpg.long_description: Side view of the bust of Nefertiti: smooth skin painted in warm tones, a finely outlined eye, red lips and a tall flat-topped blue crown with a gold band, against a pale blue background.

images/cropped-nefertiti2.jpg.alt: Front view of the bust of Nefertiti with her tall blue crown and broad painted collar, on a dark background.
images/cropped-nefertiti2.jpg.long_description: The painted limestone bust of Nefertiti seen from the front, with symmetrical features, a blue crown with a gold diadem and a collar of coloured bands, lit against a dark green background.

images/cropped-nefertiti3.jpg.alt: The bust of Nefertiti alone in a glass case in a dark room of the Neues Museum.
images/cropped-nefertiti3.jpg.long_description: The bust of Nefertiti displayed on a plinth inside a glass case in a darkened gallery of the Neues Museum in Berlin.

history.heading: A queen and a workshop
paragraphs: Nefertiti was the principal wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten, who in the fourteenth century BCE promoted the worship of the sun disc Aten and founded a new capital at Amarna. She appears in art of the period with unusual prominence, sometimes performing royal rituals herself.
The bust, of limestone covered with painted plaster, was found in 1912 in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose, where it probably served as a model for other portraits. One eye was never inlaid.

The excavation was led by Ludwig Borchardt for the German Oriental Society. In the division of finds of 1913 the bust went to the German side, and Egyptian officials have long argued that its importance was hidden from them. It has been in Berlin ever since, and is now in the Neues Museum.

geography.heading: A city in the desert
paragraphs: Amarna, known in antiquity as Akhetaten, 'Horizon of the Aten', lies on the east bank of the Nile in Middle Egypt, roughly halfway between Cairo and Luxor, in a bay of desert cliffs.
The city was built quickly and abandoned soon after Akhenaten's death, so its houses, palaces and workshops survive as low ruins in the sand, unusually well preserved for an Egyptian city.

The bust travelled from Amarna to Cairo and then to Berlin, where it has been displayed on Museum Island since 2009. Egypt's new Grand Egyptian Museum at Giza has been proposed by campaigners as a home for it.

removal.event: Excavated by a German team and exported in the division of finds, 1913

alt.long_description: A section of the Gigantomachy frieze of the Pergamon Altar in white marble: gods in flowing robes overpower giants, some with serpent legs, in deep, dramatic relief.

images/cropped-pergamon1.jpg.alt: Marble frieze of the Pergamon Altar: gods and giants fighting, with swirling drapery and broken figures.
images/cropped-pergamon1.jpg.long_description: A section of the Gigantomachy frieze of the Pergamon Altar in white marble: gods in flowing robes overpower giants, some with serpent legs, in deep, dramatic relief.

images/cropped-pergamon2.jpg.alt: Detail of the Pergamon frieze: a winged goddess and fighting figures carved in high relief.
images/cropped-pergamon2.jpg.long_description: Close view of the Pergamon Altar frieze, with a winged figure, twisting bodies and animals in high relief, the white marble casting deep shadows.

images/cropped-pergamon3.jpg.alt: The reconstructed Pergamon Altar in a large museum hall, with a wide staircase and colonnade, and visitors.
images/cropped-pergamon3.jpg.long_description: The Pergamon Altar as reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin: a broad marble staircase between two wings with columns above the frieze, in a hall lit from a glass ceiling.

history.heading: Gods against giants
paragraphs: The Great Altar of Pergamon was built in the first half of the second century BCE, probably under King Eumenes II, as a monument to Zeus and Athena. Its frieze, more than 100 metres long, shows the Gigantomachy, the battle of the Olympian gods against the giants, carved in a dramatic, emotional style.
The Attalid kings of Pergamon used art and architecture to present their city as a new Athens and themselves as defenders of Greek civilisation against the Galatians, whom they had defeated.

The German engineer Carl Humann began excavating the site in 1878. Under agreements with the Ottoman government, the frieze slabs were shipped to Berlin, where the altar was reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum. The museum has been closed for renovation since 2023.

geography.heading: A citadel above the Bakırçay valley
paragraphs: Pergamon stands on a steep hill above the modern town of Bergama, in the Izmir province of western Türkiye, about 25 kilometres from the Aegean coast, overlooking the valley of the Bakırçay river, the ancient Caicus.

Its acropolis held palaces, a famous library, temples and one of the steepest theatres of the ancient world. Pergamon and its multi-layered cultural landscape became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.
Today, on the site of the altar, only its stepped foundations remain under a group of pine trees; the frieze is in Berlin, some 2,000 kilometres away.

removal.actor: Carl Humann for the Berlin museums
removal.event: Excavated and shipped to Berlin under agreements with the Ottoman government, 1878–1886

alt.alt: Painted wooden automaton of a tiger mauling a man in European clothes, lying on a base.
alt.long_description: Tipu's Tiger seen close: a life-size wooden tiger painted with dark stripes crouches over a man in a red jacket and black hat, its jaws at his neck, set on a grey base.

images/cropped-tiputiger1.jpg.alt: Painted wooden automaton of a tiger mauling a man in European clothes, lying on a base.
images/cropped-tiputiger1.jpg.long_description: Tipu's Tiger seen close: a life-size wooden tiger painted with dark stripes crouches over a man in a red jacket and black hat, its jaws at his neck, set on a grey base.

images/cropped-tiputiger2.jpg.alt: Side view of Tipu's Tiger: the striped wooden tiger lying on top of a European soldier.
images/cropped-tiputiger2.jpg.long_description: Tipu's Tiger from the side, showing the full length of the painted wooden tiger with its long curling tail stretched over the prone figure of a European man in a red coat, on a dark wooden base.

images/cropped-tiputiger3.jpg.alt: Tipu's Tiger in a glass case in the Victoria and Albert Museum, with the organ keys visible in its side.
images/cropped-tiputiger3.jpg.long_description: The automaton displayed in a glass case at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, with the small keyboard of its organ visible in the tiger's flank and a patterned textile behind.

history.heading: A tiger for a sultan
paragraphs: Tipu Sultan ruled the Kingdom of Mysore in southern India from 1782 to 1799 and fought four wars against the British East India Company. He adopted the tiger as his emblem: tiger stripes decorated his throne, weapons and soldiers' uniforms.

Tipu's Tiger is a wooden automaton made in the 1790s. When a handle is turned, bellows inside make the tiger growl and the European man under it wail and lift his arm, while a small organ plays. It shows, in Tipu's own language of symbols, the defeat of the British.

When British forces stormed Srirangapatna in May 1799, Tipu was killed and his palace looted. The tiger was sent to London and shown at the East India Company's museum, where visitors turned its handle; it is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum.

geography.heading: An island fortress in the Kaveri
paragraphs: Srirangapatna is an island town in the Kaveri River, about 15 kilometres from the city of Mysuru in today's Karnataka. The river made it a natural fortress and the capital of Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan.
The remains of Tipu's fort, his summer palace, the Daria Daulat Bagh, with painted walls showing his victories, and his mausoleum still stand on the island.
The looted treasures travelled to Madras and then by sea to Britain, a voyage of several months. The tiger now stands in London, more than 8,000 kilometres from Srirangapatna.

removal.event: Looted by British troops after the fall of Srirangapatna, 1799

alt.alt: Ivory pendant mask of Queen Idia, with inlaid scarification lines on the forehead and a crown of small heads.
alt.long_description: The ivory mask of Queen Mother Idia: a serene face with two vertical iron-inlaid marks between the eyes, a collar and a crown decorated with small carved heads of Portuguese traders, on a grey background.

images/cropped-maskqueen1.jpg.alt: Ivory pendant mask of Queen Idia, with inlaid scarification lines on the forehead and a crown of small heads.
images/cropped-maskqueen1.jpg.long_description: The ivory mask of Queen Mother Idia: a serene face with two vertical iron-inlaid marks between the eyes, a collar and a crown decorated with small carved heads of Portuguese traders, on a grey background.

images/cropped-maskqueen2.jpg.alt: Three views of ivory Queen Idia masks, one with a red coral-bead headdress.
images/cropped-maskqueen2.jpg.long_description: Three images side by side of ivory pendant masks of Queen Mother Idia: two in pale ivory seen from the front and in profile, and one wearing a headdress of red coral beads.

images/cropped-maskqueen3.jpg.alt: The ivory mask of Queen Idia in a museum case, with other Benin objects blurred behind.
images/cropped-maskqueen3.jpg.long_description: The ivory mask of Queen Mother Idia displayed in the British Museum, sharply lit in the foreground, with Benin brass plaques and heads out of focus in cases behind.

history.heading: A mother and a warrior
paragraphs: Idia was the mother of Oba Esigie, who ruled Benin in the early sixteenth century. She is remembered for raising an army and advising her son in the war against the kingdom of Igala, and Esigie created the title of Iyoba, Queen Mother, in her honour.

The ivory mask, carved in the sixteenth century, shows her face with scarification marks between the eyes and a crown of small heads of Portuguese traders, a sign of the wealth that trade brought to Benin. It was worn by the Oba at the hip in ceremonies to honour the Queen Mother.

The mask was taken in the British attack of 1897. One version is in the British Museum and another in the Metropolitan Museum in New York. It became a symbol of African art and of Nigerian identity, and was the model for the emblem of FESTAC, the 1977 festival of African arts in Lagos.

geography.heading: The palace of Benin City
paragraphs: The mask comes from the royal palace in the centre of Benin City, in today's Edo State in southern Nigeria, where the Oba still lives and where the rituals honouring his ancestors are still held.
Ivory came from forest elephants hunted in the kingdom's territory, and carving it was the privilege of a royal guild, the Igbesanmwan.
After 1897 the mask went to London; another version reached New York. Benin City plans a new Edo museum to house returned objects near the palace.

removal.event: Seized in the British attack on Benin City, 1897

alt.alt: The Rosetta Stone, a dark granodiorite slab with a broken top, covered in lines of text, in a museum case.
alt.long_description: The Rosetta Stone in the British Museum: a large dark grey stone slab with a jagged upper edge, its polished face covered with rows of hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek inscriptions, with visitors reflected in the glass.

images/obj16-rosetta-1.jpg.alt: The Rosetta Stone, a dark granodiorite slab with a broken top, covered in lines of text, in a museum case.
images/obj16-rosetta-1.jpg.long_description: The Rosetta Stone in the British Museum: a large dark grey stone slab with a jagged upper edge, its polished face covered with rows of hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek inscriptions, with visitors reflected in the glass.

images/obj16-rosetta-2.jpg.alt: Front of the Rosetta Stone lit against black, showing the three bands of inscriptions.
images/obj16-rosetta-2.jpg.long_description: A frontal photograph of the Rosetta Stone against a black background: the hieroglyphic text in the broken top section, the Demotic in the middle and the Greek in the lowest band, carved into dark stone.

images/obj16-rosetta-3.jpg.alt: The rear of the Rosetta Stone in its glass case between two information panels.
images/obj16-rosetta-3.jpg.long_description: The Rosetta Stone seen from behind in its glass case at the British Museum, showing its rough, uninscribed back, flanked by two text panels about Egyptian writing and the stone's journey.

history.heading: One decree, three scripts
paragraphs: The Rosetta Stone preserves a decree of 196 BCE issued by Egyptian priests meeting at Memphis to honour the young king Ptolemy V. It was written in hieroglyphs, the script of temples, Demotic, the everyday Egyptian script, and Greek, the language of the Ptolemaic administration, so that everyone who mattered could read it.
The stele was later broken and reused in a wall. French soldiers found it in 1799 during Napoleon's expedition, and in 1801 the victorious British took it under the Capitulation of Alexandria.

Because the Greek could be read, scholars could compare the texts. Thomas Young identified the names of kings, and in 1822 Jean-François Champollion showed how the hieroglyphic system worked, opening three thousand years of Egyptian writing.

geography.heading: The western branch of the Nile Delta
paragraphs: Rashid lies on the Rosetta branch of the Nile, near the Mediterranean coast east of Alexandria. The Delta, fertile and densely populated, was full of temples in antiquity.
The stone may first have stood in a temple at Sais, further inland, before being moved and reused as building material in a fort near Rashid.
From Alexandria it sailed to Portsmouth in 1802 and entered the British Museum in London, about 3,500 kilometres away. A replica stands in Rashid.

removal.event: Handed from the French to the British army under the Capitulation of Alexandria, 1801

alt.alt: The Dendera zodiac seen from below: a circular sky map carved in sandstone, set into a museum ceiling.
alt.long_description: The Dendera zodiac installed overhead in the Louvre: a pale sandstone ceiling slab carved with a circle of constellations, zodiac signs and figures, supported at the corners by goddesses, seen from below in dim light.

images/obj17-dendera-1.jpg.alt: The Dendera zodiac seen from below: a circular sky map carved in sandstone, set into a museum ceiling.
images/obj17-dendera-1.jpg.long_description: The Dendera zodiac installed overhead in the Louvre: a pale sandstone ceiling slab carved with a circle of constellations, zodiac signs and figures, supported at the corners by goddesses, seen from below in dim light.

images/obj17-dendera-2.jpg.alt: The Dendera zodiac ceiling from a steep angle, with its circle of carved figures and supporting goddesses.
images/obj17-dendera-2.jpg.long_description: A view looking up at the Dendera zodiac in its Louvre setting, showing the carved disc of the sky with its figures and the kneeling and standing goddesses at its edges.

images/obj17-dendera-3.jpg.alt: Close view of the Dendera zodiac's carved figures of animals and gods around the sky disc.
images/obj17-dendera-3.jpg.long_description: Detail of the sandstone relief of the Dendera zodiac, with small carved figures of gods, animals and zodiac signs arranged in rings, lit from the side.

history.heading: A map of the Egyptian sky
paragraphs: The zodiac of Dendera is a sandstone relief of around 50 BCE from the ceiling of a chapel dedicated to Osiris on the roof of the Temple of Hathor. It shows the sky as a disc held by four goddesses: the 36 decans, the star groups the Egyptians used to tell the hours of the night, the planets and the twelve signs of the zodiac, which came to Egypt from Mesopotamia through Greek astronomy.
Its drawings, published after Napoleon's expedition, set off a debate in Europe about its age; Champollion ended it in 1822 by reading Roman-period titles in its hieroglyphs.

In 1820 Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain cut it out for the Paris collector Sébastien Louis Saulnier, using saws, chisels and gunpowder, with a permit from the government of Muhammad Ali. Louis XVIII bought it in 1821; it has been in the Louvre since 1922.

geography.heading: Hathor's temple on the bend of the Nile
paragraphs: Dendera lies on the west bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, near Qena, about 60 kilometres north of Luxor, where the river makes a wide bend. The temple of Hathor, goddess of love, music and joy, is one of the best preserved in Egypt.

Its roof was a ritual space: at the New Year priests carried the statue of Hathor up to meet the rising sun. The Osirian chapels, with their ceilings of stars, were part of the rites of the god's death and rebirth.

The block was dragged to the Nile, floated down to Alexandria and shipped to Marseille and Paris. A plaster cast now fills the ceiling at Dendera, surrounded by painted ceilings cleaned in recent years.

removal.actor: Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain for Sébastien Louis Saulnier
removal.event: Cut out for a Paris collector under a permit from Muhammad Ali's government, 1820

alt.long_description: A large rectangular Paracas mantle in red wool embroidered with repeated small human or supernatural figures in blue, green and yellow, arranged in diagonal rows, with dark corner panels.

images/obj18-paracas-1.jpg.alt: Red Paracas mantle embroidered with rows of small multicoloured figures, with dark borders at the corners.
images/obj18-paracas-1.jpg.long_description: A large rectangular Paracas mantle in red wool embroidered with repeated small human or supernatural figures in blue, green and yellow, arranged in diagonal rows, with dark corner panels.

images/obj18-paracas-2.jpg.alt: Four embroidered Paracas figures with staffs and fan-like headdresses in dark red and brown, on a light ground.
images/obj18-paracas-2.jpg.long_description: A fragment of Paracas textile with four embroidered figures, each holding a staff or knife and wearing a headdress, worked in dark red, brown and cream on a pale background.

images/obj18-paracas-3.jpg.alt: Paracas embroidery of a masked figure with serpent-like streamers in pink, blue and cream.
images/obj18-paracas-3.jpg.long_description: A Paracas embroidered fragment showing a frontal mask-like face with large eyes and streamers ending in snake heads, worked in pink, pale blue and cream on a brown ground.

history.heading: Cloth for the dead
paragraphs: The Paracas culture flourished on the south coast of Peru from about 800 BCE. In its later phase, known from the Necropolis of Wari Kayan, important people were buried seated and wrapped in dozens of layers of cloth.

The finest layers were mantles of cotton and alpaca wool embroidered with repeating figures, flying beings, animals and ritual performers in many colours. A single mantle could take thousands of hours of work.

The Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello excavated the Necropolis from 1927. In the 1930s the Swedish consul Sven Karell sent a group of textiles to Gothenburg, illegally; Sweden agreed to return them in 2013, and all 89 went back between 2014 and 2021.

geography.heading: Desert, sea and highlands
paragraphs: The Paracas peninsula lies on the southern coast of Peru, near Pisco, about 250 kilometres south of Lima, in one of the driest deserts on Earth. The cold Humboldt Current keeps rain away and fills the sea with fish, sea lions and birds.
The textiles connect coast and mountains: cotton grew in irrigated coastal valleys, while alpaca and llama wool came from the Andean highlands through exchange.
The peninsula is now a national reserve, created in 1975. The returned textiles are kept in Lima, in Peru's national collections.

removal.event: Exported illegally by the Swedish consul in Lima, 1930s

alt.alt: Old book illustration of Ngonnso', a seated carved figure covered in a dense pattern, holding a vessel on her knees.
alt.long_description: A historical photograph printed in a German publication, showing the carved figure of Ngonnso' seated on a stool, her body and headdress covered in a dense pattern, perhaps of beads or shells, holding a vessel in front of her.

images/obj19-ngonnso-1.jpg.alt: Old book illustration of Ngonnso', a seated carved figure covered in a dense pattern, holding a vessel on her knees.
images/obj19-ngonnso-1.jpg.long_description: A historical photograph printed in a German publication, showing the carved figure of Ngonnso' seated on a stool, her body and headdress covered in a dense pattern, perhaps of beads or shells, holding a vessel in front of her.

history.heading: The mother of the Nso'
paragraphs: According to Nso' history, Ngonnso' was a princess who left the kingdom of Rifum with her followers and founded a new kingdom in the grasslands of north-western Cameroon, which took her name. The figure that represents her was kept in the palace of the Fon, the Nso' king, at Kumbo.
For the Nso' she is not an object but an ancestor, connected to the well-being of the community; her absence has been felt as a wound.

The German officer Kurt von Pavel took the figure in 1902 during a campaign against the Nso', and gave it to Berlin's ethnological museum in 1903. After a campaign led by Sylvie Njobati, #BringBackNgonnso, the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation agreed in 2022 to return her; the transfer has been delayed by the conflict in Cameroon's English-speaking regions.

geography.heading: The Bamenda Grassfields
paragraphs: The Nso' kingdom lies in the Bui division of Cameroon's North-West Region, on the high plateaus of the Bamenda Grassfields, around 2,000 metres above sea level, where the climate is cool and the hills are covered in grass and farms.

The Grassfields are home to many kingdoms, each with its own Fon and palace. After the First World War the region became part of British Cameroons, and it is now one of Cameroon's two English-speaking regions.
Ngonnso' travelled from Kumbo to the coast and by sea to Berlin, about 5,000 kilometres away, where she is kept by the Ethnologisches Museum while her return is prepared.

removal.event: Seized in a German colonial campaign, 1902

alt.alt: Frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra: the Buddha preaching on a throne among monks and guardians, printed in black.
alt.long_description: The woodblock-printed frontispiece of the 868 Diamond Sutra: the Buddha seated under a canopy, preaching to the elderly monk Subhuti, surrounded by bodhisattvas, monks, guardians and two lions, with Chinese text on the left.

images/obj20-diamond-sutra-1.jpg.alt: Frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra: the Buddha preaching on a throne among monks and guardians, printed in black.
images/obj20-diamond-sutra-1.jpg.long_description: The woodblock-printed frontispiece of the 868 Diamond Sutra: the Buddha seated under a canopy, preaching to the elderly monk Subhuti, surrounded by bodhisattvas, monks, guardians and two lions, with Chinese text on the left.

images/obj20-diamond-sutra-2.jpg.alt: A long stretch of the Diamond Sutra scroll: columns of printed Chinese text next to the frontispiece.
images/obj20-diamond-sutra-2.jpg.long_description: Part of the Diamond Sutra scroll, showing columns of Chinese characters printed in black on yellowed paper beside the illustrated frontispiece.

history.heading: The oldest dated printed book
paragraphs: The Diamond Sutra is a Mahayana Buddhist text in which the Buddha teaches his disciple Subhuti about the illusory nature of the world. The Dunhuang copy is a scroll about five metres long, printed from carved wooden blocks, with a detailed picture of the Buddha preaching at the start.

Its colophon says that Wang Jie had it made for free distribution on behalf of his parents on a date that corresponds to 11 May 868. That makes it the earliest complete printed book with a date, almost six centuries before Gutenberg.

The scroll was sealed in the Library Cave at Mogao around the year 1000 with tens of thousands of other manuscripts. The cave was reopened in 1900, and in 1907 Aurel Stein obtained thousands of manuscripts, including this one, from its guardian Wang Yuanlu for a small donation.

geography.heading: An oasis on the Silk Road
paragraphs: Dunhuang is an oasis in the far west of Gansu province, where the Hexi Corridor ends and the routes of the Silk Road divide to pass north and south of the Taklamakan Desert.

The Mogao Caves, carved into a cliff about 25 kilometres south-east of the town, include around 500 decorated temples made between the fourth and fourteenth centuries. They have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
The Library Cave's contents were scattered to London, Paris, St Petersburg, Kyoto and Beijing. The International Dunhuang Programme now brings them together online.

removal.event: Sold by the caves' guardian to Aurel Stein for a small donation, 1907

alt.alt: Open page of a uigwe with printed Chinese characters in columns and a title on the right.
alt.long_description: An open volume of a Joseon royal protocol, a uigwe of the same kind as those taken from Ganghwa, with columns of printed Chinese characters on white paper and a bound spine.

images/obj21-uigwe-1.jpg.alt: Open page of a uigwe with printed Chinese characters in columns and a title on the right.
images/obj21-uigwe-1.jpg.long_description: An open volume of a Joseon royal protocol, a uigwe of the same kind as those taken from Ganghwa, with columns of printed Chinese characters on white paper and a bound spine.

images/obj21-uigwe-2.jpg.alt: Four bound volumes of a uigwe with brown covers and handwritten titles, side by side.
images/obj21-uigwe-2.jpg.long_description: Four volumes of a Joseon court uigwe with light brown paper covers, each bearing the title written in large brushed characters, fanned out side by side.

images/obj21-uigwe-3.jpg.alt: Open uigwe with line drawings of a palace courtyard and buildings seen from above.
images/obj21-uigwe-3.jpg.long_description: An open uigwe showing a double-page illustration in fine black lines: a bird's-eye view of palace buildings, courtyards and a hall prepared for a court ceremony.

history.heading: Books of royal ritual
paragraphs: Uigwe are the records the Joseon court made of its great ceremonies: royal weddings, funerals, investitures and building works. Each one lists the officials, materials and costs, and many include long painted processions, banchado, that show where every participant walked.

Several copies of each record were made. The finest, for the king's own reading, were kept from 1782 in the Oegyujanggak, an annex of the royal library that King Jeongjo built on Ganghwa Island to keep records safe from threats to the capital.

In 1866 a French naval expedition, sent after the execution of French missionaries, burned the library and took 297 volumes. The historian Park Byeong-seon found them in the Bibliothèque nationale de France in 1975, and they returned to Korea in 2011 under a renewable loan.

geography.heading: The island at the mouth of the Han
paragraphs: Ganghwa Island lies in the estuary of the Han River, north-west of Seoul, where huge tides and mudflats made it a natural fortress guarding the route to the capital.

Korean courts took refuge on the island during the Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century, and the Joseon kings ringed it with forts. It was the place where foreign fleets approached in 1866, 1871 and 1876.
The uigwe are now in the National Museum of Korea in Seoul. The Oegyujanggak building was reconstructed on Ganghwa in 2003, on an island that now faces North Korea across the water.

current.institution: National Museum of Korea (returned on loan)

removal.event: Seized by French troops, 1866

alt.alt: The blue glazed brick Ishtar Gate in the Pergamon Museum, with rows of bulls and dragons around the arch.

history.heading: The gate of Ishtar
paragraphs: Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale in the sixth century BCE. The Ishtar Gate, completed around 575 BCE, was the northern entrance to the inner city, faced with bricks glazed deep blue and decorated with moulded aurochs and mušḫuššu dragons, the animals of the gods Adad and Marduk.
Through the gate ran the Processional Way, lined with glazed lions, along which the statues of the gods were carried during the New Year festival.

Robert Koldewey's German excavations, from 1899, recovered the gate's fragments. They were divided with the Iraqi antiquities service, then under British mandate, and shipped to Berlin in 1927, where Walter Andrae reconstructed the gate in the Pergamon Museum.

geography.heading: Between the rivers
paragraphs: Babylon lies on the Euphrates in central Iraq, near Hillah, about 85 kilometres south of Baghdad, in the alluvial plain of Mesopotamia, the land 'between the rivers' Tigris and Euphrates.
In Nebuchadnezzar's time the river flowed through the city, and the Ishtar Gate opened onto the road to the north, next to the royal palace.
The gate's foundations and a modern replica are at Babylon, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2019. The reconstructed gate is in Berlin, about 3,500 kilometres away.

removal.event: Excavated by a German team and shipped in a division of finds under the British mandate, 1926–1927

history.heading: The first meeting at Kamay
paragraphs: On 29 April 1770 James Cook's Endeavour anchored in the bay the Gweagal people call Kamay. As the landing party approached, two Gweagal men stood to oppose them; Cook fired, wounding one man, who dropped or later abandoned his bark shield. The crew took the shield and about forty spears.
Bark shields were cut from the trunks of trees, often red mangrove or other hardwoods, and used in fighting and ceremony.

The shield in the British Museum was long identified as the one taken that day, but research published in 2018 questioned this. The Gweagal descendant Rodney Kelly has asked for it back. Four spears from the same landing were returned from Cambridge to the La Perouse community in 2024.

geography.heading: Kamay, Botany Bay
paragraphs: Kamay lies on the southern edge of today's Sydney, where the Georges and Cooks rivers flow into the Pacific. The Gweagal, a clan of the Dharawal people, lived on its southern shore, on the Kurnell peninsula.
The bay became famous as 'Botany Bay', the name Cook gave it for the plants his botanists collected; the British colony of 1788 was founded nearby at Sydney Cove.
Today Sydney Airport and Port Botany line the bay, while the Kamay Botany Bay National Park protects the landing site. The shield is in London, about 17,000 kilometres away.

removal.event: Taken by James Cook's crew at first contact, 1770 (identification debated)

alt.long_description: The ʻahu ʻula of Kalaniʻōpuʻu displayed flat in a case at Bishop Museum in Honolulu: a semicircular cloak of red feathers with yellow crescents and triangles; the feather helmet stands on a post at the left, with Hawaiian texts on the wall.

history.heading: Feathers of the aliʻi
paragraphs: In Hawaiian society, feather cloaks, ʻahu ʻula, and helmets, mahiole, were worn by the highest chiefs, the aliʻi. They were made by tying tiny bundles of red and yellow feathers from forest birds onto a net of olonā fibre; a single cloak could use the feathers of thousands of birds.
In January 1779 the high chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu welcomed James Cook at Kealakekua Bay and placed his own cloak and helmet on him. A few weeks later Cook was killed at the same bay.

The regalia passed through collections in England until Lord St Oswald gave them to the Dominion Museum in New Zealand in 1912. They returned to Hawaiʻi in 2016 and permanently in 2020, and are held by Bishop Museum.

geography.heading: The Kona coast
paragraphs: Kealakekua Bay is on the Kona coast, the dry western side of Hawaiʻi Island, below the cliff of Pali Kapu o Keōua, which holds royal burial caves. The Hikiau heiau, a temple linked to the god Lono, stands on its shore.
The feathers came from the upland forests of the island. Several of the birds used, such as the Hawaiʻi ʻōʻō and the mamo, are now extinct.
The regalia went from Hawaiʻi to England, then to Wellington in 1912, and back across the Pacific to Honolulu, on the island of Oʻahu.

removal.event: Given to James Cook, 1779, then sold between collectors

alt.alt: Moctezuma's headdress: a wide fan of long green quetzal feathers above a band of blue and red feathers and gold.
alt.long_description: The Mexica feather headdress in the Weltmuseum Wien, spread in a semicircle on a dark background: hundreds of long iridescent green quetzal feathers rising from bands of blue, red and brown feathers set with small gold plates.

images/obj25-penacho-1.jpg.alt: Moctezuma's headdress: a wide fan of long green quetzal feathers above a band of blue and red feathers and gold.
images/obj25-penacho-1.jpg.long_description: The Mexica feather headdress in the Weltmuseum Wien, spread in a semicircle on a dark background: hundreds of long iridescent green quetzal feathers rising from bands of blue, red and brown feathers set with small gold plates.

images/obj25-penacho-2.jpg.alt: Close view of the headdress's lower bands: blue and red feathers with rows of small gold discs.
images/obj25-penacho-2.jpg.long_description: A cropped detail of the feather headdress showing the curved bands of turquoise, red and brown feathers decorated with small gold plates, beneath the base of the green quetzal plumes.

history.heading: The art of the amanteca
paragraphs: In the Mexica (Aztec) world, fine feathers were worth more than gold. Specialist featherworkers, the amanteca, turned feathers received as tribute into headdresses, shields and garments for rulers, priests and the images of gods.

The headdress in Vienna combines about 400 long green quetzal tail feathers with feathers of the cotinga, roseate spoonbill and squirrel cuckoo and small gold plates. It is known as Moctezuma's, but there is no proof that he wore it.

After the Spanish conquest of 1519–1521, Mexica objects reached the Habsburg courts. The headdress is first recorded in 1596 at Ambras Castle in Tyrol and has been in Vienna since the nineteenth century. Mexico has asked for it; a joint Mexican-Austrian study of 2010–2012 concluded that it could not travel safely.

geography.heading: The island city in the lake
paragraphs: Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, in the high Valley of Mexico, and joined to the shore by causeways. Mexico City stands on its ruins and on the lake bed, drained after the conquest.
The headdress's materials came from far away: quetzal plumes from the cloud forests of Chiapas and Guatemala, other feathers from the tropical coasts, gold from the south and west.
It is now in the Weltmuseum Wien in the Hofburg, the former imperial palace in Vienna, about 10,000 kilometres from Mexico City. A replica is shown in the National Museum of Anthropology.

removal.event: Sent to Europe after the Spanish conquest; route unknown

images/obj26-quimbaya-3.jpg.long_description: A cast gold figure of a seated man from the Quimbaya treasure, with closed eyes, a band across the face, hands resting on the knees and ornaments on the arms and legs, gleaming against deep blue.

history.heading: Gold for the ancestors
paragraphs: The Quimbaya Treasure is a group of 122 objects of gold and tumbaga, an alloy of gold and copper, made in the middle Cauca valley of Colombia in the early centuries CE. Goldsmiths cast them by the lost-wax method and then enriched the surface so that it shone like pure gold.
The collection includes seated figures with closed eyes, some used as poporos, containers for the lime chewed with coca leaves, as well as helmets, ornaments and pins. They were found in two tombs.

Treasure hunters opened the tombs in 1890 at La Soledad, near Filandia. The Colombian government bought the objects, showed them in Madrid in 1892, and President Carlos Holguín gave them to the Spanish queen regent in 1893. In 2017 Colombia's Constitutional Court ordered the government to seek their return.

geography.heading: The coffee mountains of Quindío
paragraphs: Filandia is a small town in Quindío, on the slopes of Colombia's Central Cordillera above the Cauca valley, a region of volcanic soils, rivers carrying alluvial gold and, today, coffee farms.

The area is part of the Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011, and the regional capital, Armenia, has a museum of Quimbaya gold run by the Banco de la República.
The treasure travelled down the Magdalena River to the Caribbean and across the Atlantic to Madrid, where it is kept in the Museo de América, about 8,000 kilometres away.

removal.event: Given by Colombia's president to the Spanish queen regent, 1893

images/obj27-saint-mark-horses-2.jpg.long_description: A close view of the gilded bronze horses in the Museum of St Mark, showing their heads, collars and raised forelegs, the gilding worn in places to dark bronze.

images/obj27-saint-mark-horses-3.jpg.alt: The façade of St Mark's Basilica with the replica horses on the loggia above the main arch.
images/obj27-saint-mark-horses-3.jpg.long_description: The upper façade of St Mark's Basilica in Venice, with its Gothic pinnacles and mosaics, and the four replica bronze horses standing on the terrace above the central doorway.

history.heading: Four horses, three cities
paragraphs: The four horses are the only surviving quadriga, a team of chariot horses, from classical antiquity. They were cast in a copper-rich bronze and gilded; their date is debated, from the fourth century BCE to the second or third century CE.

They stood in Constantinople, probably in the Hippodrome, until the Venetians took them in the sack of 1204, during the Fourth Crusade. Placed on the façade of St Mark's Basilica, they became a symbol of Venice.

Napoleon took them to Paris in 1797 and placed them on the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel. After his defeat they returned to Venice in December 1815. Since the 1980s the originals have been kept inside the basilica and replicas stand outside.

geography.heading: From the Bosphorus to the lagoon
paragraphs: Constantinople, today's Istanbul, stands on the Bosphorus between Europe and Asia. The Hippodrome lay next to the imperial palace and Hagia Sophia; its site is now Sultanahmet Square.
The horses sailed through the Dardanelles and the Aegean, around Greece and up the Adriatic to Venice, a city of islands in a lagoon whose sea empire reached Crete and the Aegean.
In 1797 they crossed the Alps to Paris and in 1815 made the journey back. Today they are in the Museum of St Mark, above St Mark's Square.

removal.event: Seized by Venice in 1204 and by Napoleon in 1797

history.heading: The Adoration of the Mystic Lamb
paragraphs: The Ghent Altarpiece was commissioned by Joos Vijd and Elisabeth Borluut for their chapel in the church of St John, now St Bavo's Cathedral, and finished in 1432. An inscription names Hubert van Eyck as its first painter and his brother Jan as the one who completed it.

Its twelve oak panels, painted in oil with extraordinary detail, show the Annunciation on the closed wings and, when open, the Adoration of the Lamb of God, with God, the Virgin, John the Baptist, singing angels, and Adam and Eve.

French revolutionary troops took its central panels to Paris in 1794; the wings were sold in 1816 and bought for Berlin; two panels were stolen in 1934, and one, the Just Judges, has never been found; in 1942 Nazi Germany seized the altarpiece and hid it in the Altaussee salt mine, where the Monuments Men found it in 1945.

geography.heading: Ghent and its journeys
paragraphs: Ghent grew at the meeting of the Scheldt and Leie rivers in Flanders, and in the fifteenth century was one of the largest cities of northern Europe, rich from making cloth with English wool.
The altarpiece's absences traced a map of Europe's wars: Paris, Berlin, Pau near the Pyrenees, Neuschwanstein in Bavaria, and the salt mine at Altaussee in the Austrian Alps.
Since 2021, after a long restoration, it has been shown in a new visitor centre in St Bavo's Cathedral, in the building it was made for.

removal.event: Seized by revolutionary France, sold, stolen and seized by Nazi Germany, 1794–1942

history.heading: Gold older than Homer
paragraphs: The objects called Priam's Treasure include gold diadems with hanging chains, earrings, bracelets, thousands of gold beads, vessels of gold, silver and electrum, and bronze weapons. They belong to the settlement archaeologists call Troy II, around 2500–2300 BCE, more than a thousand years before any Trojan War.
Heinrich Schliemann announced the find in 1873 and named it after Homer's king. His account of the discovery has been questioned, and he may have put together objects found in different places.

He smuggled the treasure out of the Ottoman Empire, paid compensation after a lawsuit, and gave it to Berlin in 1881. In 1945 it was handed to the Red Army and taken to Moscow, where its presence was kept secret until the 1990s. It has been shown in the Pushkin Museum since 1996.

geography.heading: At the mouth of the Dardanelles
paragraphs: Troy occupies the mound of Hisarlık in north-western Türkiye, near the southern entrance to the Dardanelles, the strait between the Aegean and the Sea of Marmara. In the Bronze Age a bay reached close to the city; river sediment has since pushed the coast several kilometres away.
The mound holds at least nine layers of settlement. Troy has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998, and the Troy Museum, opened nearby in 2018, displays finds from the site.
The treasure has travelled from Troy to Athens, Berlin and Moscow, more than 2,000 kilometres from where it was found.

current.institution: Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts

removal.event: Smuggled out of the Ottoman Empire, 1873; seized by the Red Army, 1945

history.heading: The largest medieval manuscript
paragraphs: The Codex Gigas was written in the early thirteenth century at the small Benedictine monastery of Podlažice in Bohemia, apparently by a single scribe. It is about 92 centimetres tall and weighs around 75 kilograms.

It contains the Latin Bible, works of Josephus and Isidore of Seville, the Chronicle of the Czechs by Cosmas of Prague, medical texts, a calendar and magical formulas. A full-page picture of the Devil faces a picture of the Heavenly City, which gave it the nickname 'Devil's Bible'.

Emperor Rudolf II brought it to Prague Castle in 1594. In 1648, in the last months of the Thirty Years' War, Swedish troops seized the castle and took the codex to Stockholm. It survived the fire of the royal castle in 1697 and is now in the National Library of Sweden, which lent it to Prague in 2007–2008.

geography.heading: From Bohemia to the Baltic
paragraphs: Podlažice is a village near Chrudim in eastern Bohemia; its monastery was destroyed in the Hussite Wars of the fifteenth century. The codex then passed through the monasteries of Sedlec and Břevnov and was kept at Broumov.
Prague Castle, on a hill above the Vltava, was the residence of Rudolf II, who made Prague a centre of art and science.
In 1648 the codex was carried north, probably down the Elbe and across the Baltic, to Stockholm, more than 1,000 kilometres away, where it is displayed in the National Library in Humlegården park.

removal.event: Seized by the Swedish army at the end of the Thirty Years' War, 1648

fun.short: Il Tesoro di Priamo è un insieme di gioielli, coppe e armi d'oro dissotterrato a Troia nel 1873 da Heinrich Schliemann. Lui pensava che appartenesse al re Priamo dei racconti di Omero, ma è più antico di circa 1.000 anni! Curiosità: sparì nel 1945 e ricomparve di nascosto a Mosca.
fun.medium: Heinrich Schliemann era un uomo d'affari tedesco che amava l'Iliade di Omero, la storia della guerra di Troia. Era sicuro che Troy fosse reale, e scavò su una collina chiamata Hisarlık nel nord-ovest di Türkiye. Nel 1873 trovò un tesoro di diademi d'oro, orecchini, collane con migliaia di piccole perline, coppe d'oro e d'argento e armi di bronzo. Ha annunciato che era il tesoro del re Priamo di Troia! In effetti, proviene da una città molto più antica, costruita intorno al 2500 a.C. Schliemann lo prese segretamente dall'Impero Ottomano e successivamente lo diede a Berlino. Curiosità: alla fine della seconda guerra mondiale, il tesoro è scomparso da Berlino, e per quasi 50 anni nessuno sapeva che era nascosto in un museo di Mosca!
fun.long:
Circa 2.700 anni fa, il poeta greco Omero raccontò la storia della guerra di Troia: i Greci assediarono la città di Troia, governata dal re Priamo, per dieci anni, e finalmente si imbrogliarono con un cavallo di legno. Per molto tempo, molti pensarono che Troy fosse solo una leggenda.

Heinrich Schliemann, un uomo d'affari tedesco che era diventato ricco attraverso il commercio, credeva che fosse reale. Nel 1870 iniziò a scavare a Hisarlık, una collina vicino alle Dardanelle nell'Impero Ottomano, oggi Türkiye. I suoi operai scavarono una grande trincea attraverso la collina e scoprirono strato dopo strato di antiche città costruite uno sopra l'altro.

Nel 1873 Schliemann annunciò di aver trovato un tesoro: diademi d'oro con catene appese, orecchini, bracciali, coppe d'oro e armi d'argento e bronzo. Lo chiamò il tesoro di Priam e persino fotografò sua moglie, Sophia, indossando i gioielli d'oro, che chiamò gli "ebrei di Helen."

Ma Schliemann si sbagliava sulla data. Il tesoro proviene dagli archeologi della città chiamano Troia II, da circa 2500 a.C., più di mille anni prima che la guerra di Troia potesse accadere.

Schliemann ha anche rotto il suo accordo con il governo ottomano, che avrebbe dovuto ricevere la metà dei suoi reperti. Ha contrabbandato il tesoro ad Atene. Gli Ottomani l'hanno portato in tribunale, e lui li ha pagati. Nel 1881 diede il tesoro a Berlino.

Fatto divertente: nel 1945, mentre l'esercito sovietico catturava Berlino, il tesoro fu consegnato agli ufficiali sovietici e portato a Mosca. L'Unione Sovietica ha mantenuto questo segreto, e solo negli anni '90 il mondo ha imparato che l'oro era nel Museo Pushkin.

basic.short: Il Tesoro di Priamo, un insieme di oggetti d'oro, d'argento e di bronzo di Troia II (c. 2500–2300 a.C.), fu trovato da Heinrich Schliemann nel 1873 e portato di contrabbando fuori dall'Impero ottomano. Donato a Berlino nel 1881, fu preso dall'Armata Rossa nel 1945 e negli anni Novanta si scoprì che era al Museo Puškin di Mosca.
basic.medium: Nel 1873 Heinrich Schliemann scoprì un insieme di oggetti metallici a Hisarlık, nell'Anatolia nord-occidentale, che identificò come il sito del Troia di Omero. Il tesoro comprendeva diademi d'oro, orecchini, bracciali e migliaia di perline, vasi d'oro, argento ed electrum, e armi di bronzo. Schliemann la chiamò "Il tesoro di Priam," ma appartiene al livello conosciuto come Troia II, datato a circa 2500 a.C. Contrariamente al suo permesso, che gli imponeva di condividere i suoi ritrovamenti con lo Stato ottomano, Schliemann contrabbandava il tesoro ad Atene. Dopo una causa, ha pagato l'indennizzo del governo ottomano. Nel 1881 donò la sua collezione a Berlino. Nel 1945 il tesoro fu consegnato all'Armata Rossa e portato a Mosca. La sua esistenza è stata tenuta segreta fino ai primi anni '90, ed è stata esposta al Museo Pushkin dal 1996. La Germania e Türkiye lo sostengono entrambi.
basic.long:
Hisarlık, un tumulo vicino all'ingresso delle Dardanelle nell'Anatolia nord-occidentale, era stato proposto come sito di Troia prima che Heinrich Schliemann iniziasse a scavare lì nel 1870. Schliemann, un mercante che aveva fatto una fortuna nel commercio, era determinato a dimostrare che il Troy di Omero era storico. I suoi scavi, con grandi trincee tagliate attraverso il tumulo, hanno rivelato una sequenza di città sovrapposte, ma anche distrutto gran parte del loro contesto archeologico.

Nel 1873 Schliemann trovò un tesoro di oggetti vicino ad un muro della città primitiva, che annunciò come il tesoro del re Priamo. Esso includeva diademi d'oro, orecchini, bracciali, perline e migliaia di piccole perle d'oro, così come vasi d'oro, argento, electrum e bronzo, e armi di bronzo. Il tesoro appartiene al livello ora chiamato Troia II, intorno al 2500 a.C., molto prima di qualsiasi guerra storica di Troia. Anche il resoconto di Schliemann di come è stato trovato è stato messo in discussione.

Il permesso di Schliemann gli ha richiesto di dare metà dei suoi reperti al Museo Imperiale di Costantinopoli. Invece, ha contrabbandato il tesoro ad Atene. Il governo ottomano lo fece causa in una corte greca, e nel 1875 il caso fu risolto quando Schliemann pagò un risarcimento al Museo Imperiale. Nel 1881 donò il tesoro e gli altri ritrovamenti di Troia alla città di Berlino.

Durante la Seconda Guerra Mondiale, il tesoro fu conservato in una torre a picco allo Zoo di Berlino. Nel 1945 i funzionari del museo lo consegnarono all'esercito sovietico, e fu portato a Mosca. Per decenni le autorità sovietiche negarono di sapere dov'era. Nei primi anni '90, dopo le indagini dei giornalisti, la Russia ha confermato che si trovava nel Museo Pushkin, dove è stato esposto dal 1996. La Germania sostiene che la proprietà sia stata rimossa illegalmente dal tempo di guerra; Türkiye sostiene che sia stata esportata illegalmente dall'Impero Ottomano.

expert.short: Il Tesoro di Priamo è stato spostato tre volte: portato di contrabbando fuori dall'Impero ottomano da Schliemann nel 1873, sottratto a Berlino come trofeo sovietico nel 1945 e rivendicato sia dalla Germania sia dalla Turchia. La legge russa del 1998 sui beni culturali trasferiti ne fa, per il diritto russo, proprietà dello Stato.
expert.medium: Il tesoro di Troia II, variamente interpretato come un deposito unico o un assemblaggio compilato da diversi reperti, è stato erroneamente identificato da Schliemann con Troia di Omero, una pretesa il suo collaboratore Wilhelm Dörpfeld successivamente corretto. La sua esportazione ha violato i termini del firman di Schliemann e il regolamento ottomano allora in vigore; la causa di Atene si è conclusa nel 1875 con un accordo che il lato ottomano ha accettato, ma che più tardi Turco sostiene considerare come riparazione incompleta. Donato a Berlino nel 1881, il tesoro fu consegnato da Wilhelm Unverzagt alle forze sovietiche nel maggio 1945 e portato a Mosca da una brigata di trofei. La sua posizione è stata nascosta fino alle rivelazioni di Konstantin Akinsha e Grigorii Kozlov nel 1991. La Germania invoca il trattato tedesco del 1990 e il diritto internazionale sui traslochi in tempo di guerra; la Russia si basa sulla legge federale del 1998 sui beni culturali sfollati a seguito della seconda guerra mondiale, che tratta tali beni come restituzione compensativa. La richiesta di Türkiye si basa sull'esportazione illecita originaria, causando una controversia a strati con tre ricorrenti.
expert.long:
Il tesoro trovato da Heinrich Schliemann nel 1873 appartiene al livello di Troia II, datato alla metà del terzo millennio a.C. Sia che si trattasse di un unico deposito o di un insieme di oggetti provenienti da diversi contesti combinati da Schliemann rimane discusso, come fa il suo racconto della sua scoperta. La sua identificazione con il Troia di Priam, centrale per l'auto-presentazione di Schliemann, fu abbandonata dopo che il suo collaboratore Wilhelm Dörpfeld dimostrò che i livelli dell'età del bronzo tardo erano molto più tardi.

Il primo spostamento fu l'esportazione illecita dall'Impero Ottomano. Il firmano di Schliemann gli chiese di condividere i reperti con il Museo Imperiale, il cui direttore Philipp Anton Dethier cercò di far rispettare le norme ottomane. Schliemann contrabbandò il tesoro ad Atene, e il governo ottomano lo fece causa davanti ad una corte greca. Nel 1875 le parti si stabilirono: Schliemann pagò un risarcimento al Museo Imperiale e mantenne il tesoro. L'episodio contribuì alla più rigorosa legge ottomana sulle antichità del 1884, redatta sotto la guida di Osman Hamdi Bey. Da allora i ricorrenti turchi hanno sostenuto che l'accordo non legittimava un'esportazione contraria alla legge ottomana.

Il secondo spostamento fu la rimozione in tempo di guerra. Donato a Berlino nel 1881, il tesoro è stato conservato durante la seconda guerra mondiale nella torre di Flak allo Zoo. Nel maggio 1945 il preistorico Wilhelm Unverzagt lo cedette alle forze sovietiche, e le brigate trofeo lo trasportarono a Mosca, parte di una sistematica rimozione della proprietà culturale dalla Germania come risarcimento per la distruzione nazista nell'Unione Sovietica. La sua posizione è stata nascosta per quasi mezzo secolo fino a quando Konstantin Akinsha e Grigorii Kozlov hanno rivelato nel 1991 che si è tenuto nel Museo Pushkin; Russia confermato questo nel 1993, e il tesoro è stato esposto lì dal 1996.

Il terzo livello è l'attuale controversia legale. La Germania rivendica il tesoro ai sensi del trattato di buon vicinato del 1990 con l'Unione Sovietica e dell'accordo culturale del 1992 con la Russia, che prevedono la restituzione di beni culturali usciti illecitamente, e del regolamento dell'Aia che vieta il sequestro di beni culturali. La legge federale russa del 1998 sui beni culturali trasferiti nell'URSS a seguito della seconda guerra mondiale dichiara tali beni proprietà dello Stato russo, come restituzione compensatoria per perdite in tempo di guerra. Türkiye ha affermato che, se il tesoro dovesse lasciare la Russia, la sua affermazione avrebbe la precedenza come stato di origine.

Il caso è quindi una controversia stratificata in cui ogni ricorrente si basa su un momento storico diverso: l'esportazione illecita del 1873, la donazione del 1881, la rimozione del 1945. Essa illustra come gli spostamenti successivi possono generare legittimità concorrenti, e come la restituzione richiede la scelta di quale passato riparare.

it.title: Tesoro di Priamo – c. 2500–2300 a.C.
it.caption-2: Allora: Troia (Hisarlık, Impero ottomano), Turchia - Oggi: Mosca, Russia

fun.medium: Heinrich Schliemann était un homme d'affaires allemand qui aimait Homer's Iliad, l'histoire de la guerre de Troie. Il était sûr que Troy était réel, et il a creusé dans une colline appelée Hisarlık dans le nord-ouest de Türkiye. En 1873, il trouva un corbeau de diadèmes d'or, des boucles d'oreilles, des colliers avec des milliers de petites perles, des coupes d'or et d'argent, et des armes de bronze. Il a annoncé que c'était le trésor du roi Priam de Troie! En fait, il vient d'une ville beaucoup plus ancienne, construite entre 2500 et 2300 avant JC. Schliemann l'a secrètement sortie de l'Empire ottoman et l'a ensuite donnée à Berlin. Fait amusant : à la fin de la Seconde Guerre mondiale, le trésor a disparu de Berlin, et pendant près de 50 ans, personne ne savait qu'il était caché dans un musée de Moscou !
fun.long:
Il y a environ 2 700 ans, le poète grec Homer racontait l'histoire de la guerre de Troie : les Grecs assiégeaient la ville de Troie, gouvernée par le roi Priam, pendant dix ans, et enfin s'emparaient d'un cheval de bois. Pendant longtemps, beaucoup de gens pensaient que Troy n'était qu'une légende.

Heinrich Schliemann, un homme d'affaires allemand qui s'était enrichi par le commerce, croyait que c'était réel. En 1870, il commence à creuser à Hisarlık, une colline près des Dardanelles dans l'Empire ottoman, aujourd'hui Türkiye. Ses ouvriers creusèrent une énorme tranchée à travers la colline et découvrirent une couche d'anciennes villes construites l'une sur l'autre.

En 1873, Schliemann annonça qu'il avait trouvé un trésor : des diadèmes d'or avec des chaînes suspendues, des boucles d'oreilles, des bracelets, des coupes d'or et d'argent et des armes de bronze. Il l'a appelé Trésor de Priam et a même photographié sa femme, Sophia, portant les bijoux en or, qu'il a appelé les "Juifs d'Hélène".

Mais Schliemann avait tort à propos de la date. Le trésor provient des archéologues de la ville appelés Troy II, d'environ 2500 à 2300 avant notre ère, plus de mille ans avant la guerre de Troie.

Schliemann a également rompu son accord avec le gouvernement ottoman, qui était censé recevoir la moitié de ses découvertes. Il a fait passer le trésor à Athènes. Les Ottomans l'emmenèrent devant les tribunaux, et il leur paya une compensation. En 1881, il donna le trésor à Berlin.

Fait amusant: en 1945, alors que l'armée soviétique s'empara de Berlin, le trésor fut remis aux officiers soviétiques et emmené à Moscou. L'Union soviétique a gardé ce secret, et ce n'est que dans les années 90 que le monde a appris que l'or se trouvait au Musée Pouchkine.

basic.medium: En 1873, Heinrich Schliemann découvrit une réserve d'objets métalliques à Hisarlık, dans le nord-ouest de l'Anatolie, qu'il identifia comme le site de la Troie d'Homère. Il comprenait des diadèmes d'or, des boucles d'oreilles, des bracelets et des milliers de perles, des vases d'or, d'argent et d'électricité, et des armes de bronze. Schliemann l'a nommé Trésor de Priam, mais il appartient au niveau connu sous le nom de Troy II, daté d'environ 2500 à 2300 avant JC. Contrairement à son permis, qui l'obligeait à partager ses découvertes avec l'État ottoman, Schliemann fit entrer le trésor en contrebande à Athènes. Après un procès, il a payé l'indemnisation du gouvernement ottoman. En 1881, il fit don de sa collection à Berlin. En 1945, le trésor fut remis à l'armée rouge et emmené à Moscou. Son existence a été gardée secrète jusqu'au début des années 90, et elle est exposée au Musée Pouchkine depuis 1996. L'Allemagne et Türkiye le prétendent tous les deux.
basic.long:
Hisarlık, un monticule près de l'entrée des Dardanelles dans le nord-ouest de l'Anatolie, avait été proposé comme le site de Troy avant Heinrich Schliemann commencé à y excaver en 1870. Schliemann, un marchand qui avait fait fortune dans le commerce, était déterminé à prouver que la Troie d'Homère était historique. Ses fouilles, avec de grandes tranchées coupées à travers le monticule, ont révélé une séquence de villes superposées, mais ont également détruit une grande partie de leur contexte archéologique.

En 1873, Schliemann trouva une réserve d'objets près d'un mur de la ville primitive, qu'il annonça comme le trésor du roi Priam. Il comprenait des diadèmes d'or, des boucles d'oreilles, des bracelets, des épingles et des milliers de petites perles d'or, ainsi que des vaisseaux d'or, d'argent, d'électricité et de bronze, et des armes de bronze. Le corbeau appartient au niveau maintenant appelé Troy II, vers 2500–2300 avant JC, bien plus tôt que n'importe quelle guerre de Troie historique possible. Le récit de Schliemann sur la façon dont il a été trouvé a également été remis en question.

Le permis de Schliemann l'obligeait à remettre la moitié de ses découvertes au Musée impérial de Constantinople. Au lieu de cela, il a fait passer le trésor à Athènes. Le gouvernement ottoman l'a poursuivi devant une cour grecque et, en 1875, l'affaire a été réglée lorsque Schliemann a versé une indemnisation au Musée impérial. En 1881, il fit don du trésor et de ses autres trouvailles à la ville de Berlin.
